topics.title: Lucy: The Fossil That Changed Everything

hook.text: In 1974, a team in Ethiopia found 40 percent of a skeleton from 3.2 million years ago. They named her Lucy.

buildup.text: Lucy was an Australopithecus afarensis — three and a half feet tall with a small brain but upright legs.

discovery.text: Her knee and pelvis proved she walked upright. Walking came millions of years before big brains evolved.

twist.text: The team celebrated the find while playing 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds.' The Beatles song gave her a name.

climax.text: Lucy showed that human evolution did not start with intelligence. It started with standing up.

punchline.text: We walked before we thought. Lucy proved it with her knees.

quiz.question: What did Lucy's skeleton prove about human evolution?
options: Big brains evolved before upright walking
Upright walking came millions of years before big brains
Early hominins could both walk and swing through trees equally well

hook.text: In Tanzania, 3.6-million-year-old footprints show two early humans walking side by side through volcanic ash.

buildup.text: Mary Leakey discovered the prints in 1978. They were preserved when wet ash from a nearby eruption hardened like cement.

discovery.text: The prints have arches and forward-pointing toes — unmistakable signs of upright bipedal walking.

twist.text: A smaller third set of tracks suggests a child was walking alongside the adults. A family stroll, 3.6 million years ago.

climax.text: These are the oldest confirmed footprints of human ancestors — half a million years older than Lucy.

punchline.text: A family walked through ash 3.6 million years ago.

quiz.question: How were the Laetoli footprints preserved?
options: They were carved into rock by flowing water
Wet volcanic ash hardened like cement around the impressions
They were covered by a layer of mud during a flood

hook.text: Homo erectus was the first human species to leave Africa. They made it to Indonesia, China, and Georgia.

buildup.text: They appeared around 1.9 million years ago with larger brains, longer legs, and the ability to control fire.

discovery.text: Java Man, found in 1891, was the first Homo erectus fossil discovered. It proved humans had deep Asian roots.

twist.text: Homo erectus survived for nearly 2 million years — far longer than our own species has existed so far.

climax.text: A 2019 study suggests they may have survived on Java until 100,000 years ago — overlapping with modern humans.

punchline.text: They left Africa first, survived the longest, and walked the farthest.

quiz.question: Why is Homo erectus significant in human evolution?
options: They were the first species to create written language
They were the first human species to leave Africa
They evolved directly into modern humans in Europe

topics.title: Neanderthals: Not the Brutes We Imagined

hook.text: Neanderthals buried their dead, made jewelry, and possibly painted caves. They were not stupid cavemen.

buildup.text: They lived across Europe and western Asia for over 300,000 years, surviving ice ages with sophisticated tools.

discovery.text: At Shanidar Cave in Iraq, a burial was found surrounded by pollen — suggesting the body was covered in flowers.

twist.text: DNA proves that most people outside Africa carry 1–4% Neanderthal genes. They did not just die out — they mixed with us.

climax.text: In 2018, cave paintings in Spain were dated to 65,000 years ago — made by Neanderthals, not modern humans.

punchline.text: They painted art, buried their dead, and live on in our DNA.

quiz.question: What did DNA analysis reveal about Neanderthals and modern humans?
options: Neanderthals and humans never interbred or interacted
Most people outside Africa carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA
Neanderthals were a subspecies of Homo sapiens

hook.text: An entire species of ancient human was identified from a single finger bone found in a Siberian cave.

buildup.text: In 2010, DNA from the bone revealed a previously unknown human species that split from Neanderthals 400,000 years ago.

discovery.text: The Denisovans lived across Asia. Their DNA survives in modern Tibetans, helping them breathe at high altitude.

twist.text: Only five Denisovan fossils have ever been found. We know more about their genome than about what they looked like.

climax.text: A jaw found in a Tibetan cave at 10,000 feet confirms Denisovans thrived in extreme environments.

punchline.text: We mapped their DNA before we found their face.

quiz.question: How were the Denisovans first discovered?
options: A complete skeleton was found in a Chinese limestone cave
DNA from a single finger bone in a Siberian cave revealed an unknown species
Cave paintings depicting an unknown human species led to the search

topics.title: The Flores Hobbit: A Tiny Human

hook.text: On a remote Indonesian island, archaeologists found a human species that stood just three and a half feet tall.

buildup.text: Homo floresiensis was found in Liang Bua cave in 2003. They had small brains but made stone tools and hunted pygmy.

discovery.text: They survived on Flores until at least 50,000 years ago — meaning they overlapped with modern humans in the region.

twist.text: Local legends describe small forest people called Ebu Gogo. Some wonder if folk memory preserved a real species.

climax.text: Island dwarfism explains their size — isolation on small islands shrinks large animals and can shrink humans too.

punchline.text: A real human species the size of a toddler hunted elephants on an island.

quiz.question: What likely explains the small size of Homo floresiensis?
options: They were children of a normal-sized species
Island dwarfism caused by long-term isolation on a small island
A genetic disease that stunted their growth

hook.text: The oldest known stone tools are 3.3 million years old. They were made before our genus Homo even existed.

buildup.text: Oldowan tools from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania are simple cobbles with a few flakes knocked off to create an edge.

discovery.text: Experiments show it takes real skill to knap stone consistently. Early toolmakers understood angles and fracture lines.

twist.text: Chimpanzees use rocks to crack nuts but cannot produce sharp flakes. The leap to stone tools was a cognitive revolution.

climax.text: Oldowan technology stayed unchanged for over a million years. The first invention was also the longest lasting.

punchline.text: The first technology lasted a million years. Your phone lasts two.

quiz.question: What makes Oldowan stone tools significant?
options: They are the most complex stone tools ever discovered
They are the oldest known tools and lasted over a million years unchanged
They were the first tools made from metal instead of wood

topics.title: The Acheulean Handaxe: A Million-Year Design

hook.text: The same teardrop-shaped stone tool was made on three continents for over a million years. Nobody knows exactly why.

buildup.text: Acheulean handaxes appear from Africa to Europe to India. They are symmetrical, often beautiful.

discovery.text: Making one requires planning: choosing the right stone, removing flakes in sequence, and shaping both sides evenly.

twist.text: Many handaxes show no signs of use. Some archaeologists think they were displays of skill — prehistoric showing off.

climax.text: A handaxe found in Norfolk was embedded in an elephant bone. Others were used for butchering large animals.

punchline.text: One tool design lasted a million years across three continents.

quiz.question: Why do some archaeologists think unused handaxes were made?
options: They were religious objects placed in temples
They may have been displays of skill — prehistoric showing off
They were stored as emergency tools for future use

hook.text: Controlling fire was the most important thing humans ever did. It changed our bodies, our brains, and our diet.

buildup.text: The earliest possible hearths date to one million years ago at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa.

discovery.text: Cooking breaks down tough plant fibers and kills parasites in meat.

twist.text: Richard Wrangham argues that cooking shrank our guts and grew our brains. Fire literally reshaped human anatomy.

climax.text: Fire also created campfires — the first gathering place. Socializing around flames may have driven language evolution.

punchline.text: Fire cooked our food, grew our brains, and started our conversations.

quiz.question: How did cooking with fire affect human evolution according to Richard Wrangham?
options: It allowed humans to survive in colder climates
It shrank our guts and allowed our brains to grow larger
It eliminated the need for stone tools

hook.text: Wooden spears from 400,000 years ago were found in a German coal mine — they were sharpened, balanced, and deadly.

buildup.text: The Schöningen spears were found alongside butchered horse bones. Hunters ambushed herds at a lakeside.

discovery.text: The spears are as long as modern javelins and weighted for throwing. These were designed weapons, not sharpened sticks.

twist.text: This was 200,000 years before Homo sapiens appeared. Homo heidelbergensis made them — an ancestor, not modern humans.

climax.text: Group hunting requires coordination, planning, and communication. Weapon design implies language existed very early.

punchline.text: They designed balanced throwing weapons 400,000 years ago.

quiz.question: What is remarkable about the Schöningen spears?
options: They are the oldest metal weapons ever found
They were balanced for throwing, 200,000 years before Homo sapiens existed
They were made from a stone material not found in Germany

hook.text: Clothes rot away. So how do archaeologists know when humans started wearing them? They studied lice.

buildup.text: Body lice evolved from head lice when humans started wearing clothes — giving lice a new habitat to colonize.

discovery.text: DNA analysis dates the split between head lice and body lice to about 170,000 years ago — the likely start of clothing.

twist.text: The oldest sewing needle is 50,000 years old, found in a Denisovan cave.

climax.text: Clothing was not about modesty. It was survival technology that let humans leave Africa and survive ice ages.

punchline.text: We figured out when humans got dressed by asking when lice moved in.

quiz.question: How did scientists determine when humans first wore clothing?
options: They carbon-dated the oldest preserved fabric fragments
They analyzed when body lice evolved from head lice using DNA
They found cave paintings depicting people wearing animal skins

topics.title: Bone Flutes and the Oldest Music

hook.text: A 40,000-year-old flute carved from a vulture bone is the oldest known musical instrument. It still plays notes.

buildup.text: The flute was found in Hohle Fels cave in Germany alongside carved figurines and early jewelry.

discovery.text: It has five finger holes and plays a recognizable pentatonic scale — the same scale used in music worldwide today.

twist.text: Music serves no obvious survival function. Its existence 40,000 years ago suggests human culture was already rich and.

climax.text: Researchers played a replica and produced hauntingly beautiful tones. Ice Age people made real music, not just noise.

punchline.text: Forty thousand years ago, someone carved a flute and played a song.

quiz.question: What is significant about the Hohle Fels bone flute?
options: It proves that only Homo sapiens were capable of creating art
It plays a pentatonic scale still used in music worldwide today
It was made from a mammoth tusk, showing advanced carving skills

hook.text: Four teenagers chasing a dog into a hole in 1940 discovered the most spectacular cave paintings in the world.

buildup.text: Lascaux's walls are covered with over 600 paintings of horses, bulls, deer, and one mysterious bird-headed man.

discovery.text: The paintings are 17,000 years old. Artists used mineral pigments blown through bone tubes for shading and texture.

twist.text: Tourist breath caused mold to attack the paintings. Lascaux was sealed in 1963.

climax.text: No one knows why they were painted. Hunting magic, storytelling, or spiritual rituals — all theories remain unproven.

punchline.text: Teenagers found the Sistine Chapel of the Ice Age. Now no one is allowed inside.

quiz.question: Why was Lascaux Cave sealed to the public in 1963?
options: The French government wanted to charge higher admission fees
Tourist breath caused mold that was damaging the paintings
Vandals scratched their names into several of the panels

hook.text: Across Europe, archaeologists found dozens of small female figurines with exaggerated features carved 30,000 years ago.

buildup.text: The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria in 1908, is four inches tall and carved from limestone with no face.

discovery.text: Similar figurines were found from France to Siberia, spanning 10,000 years and thousands of miles.

twist.text: Their meaning is fiercely debated: fertility symbols, self-portraits, goddesses, or something we cannot comprehend.

climax.text: A 2020 study proposed they represent ideal body fat for surviving ice ages — a symbol of health, not beauty.

punchline.text: We call them Venuses. The people who carved them never told us what they meant.

quiz.question: What is one recent theory about the Venus figurines' meaning?
options: They were children's toys traded along migration routes
They represent ideal body fat for surviving ice age conditions
They are portraits of specific tribal leaders

topics.title: The Chauvet Cave: Art Before Civilization

hook.text: Cave paintings in southern France are 36,000 years old — twice as old as Lascaux — and far more sophisticated.

buildup.text: Chauvet Cave was discovered in 1994 by three hikers. Lions, rhinos, and bears cover the walls in dynamic poses.

discovery.text: Artists used shading, perspective, and even motion lines. One panel shows a bison with eight legs to suggest running.

twist.text: The cave had been sealed by a rockfall 20,000 years ago. The air inside was untouched, the art pristine.

climax.text: Chauvet proves that artistic genius did not evolve gradually. Full sophistication appeared right from the start.

punchline.text: The oldest known art is also among the best.

quiz.question: What makes Chauvet Cave art surprising to researchers?
options: It uses metal pigments not found in later cave art
It shows full artistic sophistication from the very start, not gradual improvement
It depicts scenes of farming that predate known agriculture

topics.title: The First Burials: When Death Got Meaning

hook.text: The oldest known deliberate burial is over 78,000 years old. A child was placed in a shallow grave in a Kenyan cave.

buildup.text: The child, named Mtoto, was about three years old. The body was carefully positioned on its side with flexed legs.

discovery.text: The grave was inside Panga ya Saidi cave. Soil analysis showed the pit was deliberately dug and the body covered.

twist.text: Neanderthals also buried their dead. Intentional burial may not be unique to Homo sapiens after all.

climax.text: Deliberate burial implies belief in something beyond death — or at least a bond too strong to abandon a body.

punchline.text: Seventy-eight thousand years ago, someone buried a child with care.

quiz.question: Why is the burial of 'Mtoto' in Kenya significant?
options: It is the only burial found with written inscriptions
It is the oldest known deliberate human burial in Africa
It contained the earliest known grave goods made of metal

hook.text: Perforated shell beads from Morocco are 150,000 years old — the oldest known jewelry in the world.

buildup.text: The shells were pierced with stone points and strung together. Some show traces of red ochre pigment.

discovery.text: Similar beads appear in South Africa, Israel, and Algeria. Jewelry-making emerged independently across three continents.

twist.text: Jewelry serves no survival purpose. Its existence proves symbolic thinking — the ability to assign meaning to objects.

climax.text: Symbolic thinking is the cognitive leap behind language, art, religion, and civilization. Beads may mark its beginning.

punchline.text: A hole in a shell may be the first sign that humans could think in symbols.

quiz.question: Why are ancient shell beads important to understanding human evolution?
options: They prove early humans had advanced trade networks
They demonstrate symbolic thinking — the ability to assign meaning to objects
They show early humans lived exclusively near coastlines

hook.text: The Sahara Desert is covered in rock art showing hippos, crocodiles, and cattle herders. It was once green.

buildup.text: Between 10,000 and 4,000 years ago, the Sahara had lakes, rivers, and grasslands supporting millions of people.

discovery.text: Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria has over 15,000 engravings and paintings spanning 8,000 years of climate and culture.

twist.text: The art shows the transition from hunting to herding in real time. As the climate dried, animals in the art changed too.

climax.text: When the Sahara dried completely, people migrated to the Nile Valley — possibly seeding Egyptian civilization.

punchline.text: The Sahara recorded its own death in pictures.

quiz.question: What does Saharan rock art reveal about the region's past?
options: The Sahara was always a desert with nomadic populations
The region was once green with lakes, rivers, and millions of people
Ancient armies used the Sahara as a battlefield

hook.text: Farming was not an invention. It was a slow accident that took thousands of years and made life worse for most people.

buildup.text: Around 12,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, people began planting wild wheat and barley instead of just gathering.

discovery.text: Archaeobotanists found the transition in seed size. Cultivated seeds are larger because farmers selected the biggest.

twist.text: Skeletons from early farmers show worse health than their hunter-gatherer ancestors: shorter, sicker, and harder worked.

climax.text: Farming supported more people per acre but demanded more labor. Humanity traded quality of life for quantity of people.

punchline.text: Farming made civilization possible and individual life worse.

quiz.question: What did skeletons reveal about early farmers' health?
options: They were taller and stronger than hunter-gatherers
They were shorter, sicker, and harder worked than hunter-gatherers
Their health was identical to previous populations

hook.text: Dogs were the first domesticated animal — tamed from wolves at least 15,000 years ago, long before farming began.

buildup.text: Wolves that tolerated humans scavenged from campsites. Over generations, the friendliest ones were kept and bred.

discovery.text: A 14,000-year-old burial in Germany contains a puppy placed beside a human. The bond was already deep.

twist.text: Domestication changed wolf anatomy: skulls shortened, teeth shrank, and floppy ears appeared — the 'domestication.

climax.text: Dogs helped humans hunt, herd, and guard. Some researchers argue we could not have built civilization without them.

punchline.text: We think we tamed wolves. They may have tamed us first.

quiz.question: What physical changes occurred in wolves during domestication?
options: They became larger and more aggressive
Skulls shortened, teeth shrank, and floppy ears appeared
Their fur became waterproof and their legs grew longer

hook.text: Jericho may be the oldest continuously inhabited city on Earth. People have lived there for over 11,000 years.

buildup.text: The earliest settlement had round mud-brick houses and a massive stone tower dating to 8000 BCE — the oldest known.

discovery.text: The tower is 28 feet tall and required organized labor. A small farming village built a monument before pyramids.

twist.text: Residents plastered and painted skulls of their dead and displayed them in houses — an ancestor worship practice.

climax.text: Jericho shows that permanent settlement, monumental building, and complex ritual all appeared before pottery was.

punchline.text: They built a tower 10,000 years ago. They had not yet invented a clay pot.

quiz.question: What makes Jericho's stone tower remarkable?
options: It is the tallest ancient structure in the Middle East
It is the oldest known tower, built before pottery was invented
It was used as an astronomical observatory

hook.text: The oldest known pottery was made 20,000 years ago in China — by hunter-gatherers, not farmers.

buildup.text: Fragments from Xianrendong Cave show simple, thick-walled vessels used for cooking food over fire.

discovery.text: Residue analysis found traces of fish, meat, and plants. Pottery let people boil food for the first time — unlocking.

twist.text: Pottery was invented independently in Japan, China, Africa, and the Middle East — four separate inventions of the same.

climax.text: Pottery enabled food storage, fermentation, and brewing. Beer, bread, and cheese all depend on a clay container.

punchline.text: A clay pot changed the human diet forever.

quiz.question: What is surprising about the oldest known pottery?
options: It was made by early farmers in Mesopotamia
It was made 20,000 years ago by hunter-gatherers in China
It was used exclusively for religious ceremonies

topics.title: The Spread of Farming Across Europe

hook.text: Farming spread across Europe in about 2,500 years. Ancient DNA shows the farmers came too — they did not just share.

buildup.text: Neolithic farmers migrated from Anatolia starting around 7000 BCE, bringing wheat, barley, sheep, and cattle.

discovery.text: DNA from ancient skeletons shows that European hunter-gatherers and incoming farmers were genetically distinct.

twist.text: In some areas, hunter-gatherers vanished entirely. In others, they mixed with farmers. The pattern varied by region.

climax.text: Modern Europeans carry DNA from both groups. The farming revolution was also a migration and a mixing event.

punchline.text: Farming did not just spread across Europe. The farmers themselves walked there.

quiz.question: What did ancient DNA reveal about the spread of farming in Europe?
options: European hunter-gatherers invented farming independently
Genetically distinct farmers migrated from Anatolia, bringing agriculture with them
Farming spread through trade without any population movement

hook.text: Before bronze, before iron, people figured out that green rocks could be melted into copper — and shaped into tools.

buildup.text: The oldest smelted copper comes from Serbia, dating to about 5000 BCE. It was soft, but it could be resharpened.

discovery.text: Copper axes and ornaments spread through Europe and the Middle East. Metalworking became a specialized craft.

twist.text: Ötzi the Iceman carried a copper axe in 3300 BCE. Chemical analysis traced its copper to Tuscany — 300 miles away.

climax.text: Copper was too soft for heavy work but proved that metals could be extracted from rock. Bronze and iron followed.

punchline.text: Someone melted a green rock and got a knife.

quiz.question: What did Ötzi the Iceman's copper axe reveal?
options: Copper tools were only used by elite warriors
Chemical analysis traced its copper 300 miles to Tuscany, showing long-distance trade
Copper was more durable than bronze for cutting tools

topics.title: Stonehenge: The Mystery That Won't Die

hook.text: Stonehenge took 1,500 years to build. The biggest stones weigh 25 tons and were dragged 25 miles to the site.

buildup.text: The smaller bluestones came from Wales — 150 miles away. How they were transported remains one of archaeology's biggest.

discovery.text: The stones align with the sunrise on the summer solstice and sunset on the winter solstice — a deliberate solar.

twist.text: Cremated remains of over 60 people were buried at Stonehenge. It was also a cemetery — not just an observatory.

climax.text: Chemical analysis of the bones shows people came from as far as Wales and the Mediterranean to be buried there.

punchline.text: People traveled hundreds of miles to be buried at Stonehenge.

quiz.question: What did analysis of cremated remains at Stonehenge reveal?
options: All burials were local farmers from the Salisbury Plain
People came from as far as Wales and the Mediterranean to be buried there
Only royalty and priests were allowed to be interred at the site

hook.text: In Brittany, France, over 3,000 standing stones march in perfect rows across the countryside for two miles.

buildup.text: The Carnac stones were erected between 4500 and 3300 BCE — before Stonehenge, the pyramids, or writing.

discovery.text: The alignments run east to west in parallel rows. Some stones are 12 feet tall; others barely reach knee height.

twist.text: Nobody knows their purpose. Theories include astronomical markers, ritual pathways, and earthquake detectors.

climax.text: Local legend says the stones are Roman soldiers turned to stone by Merlin. Archaeology offers no better explanation yet.

punchline.text: Three thousand stones in perfect rows. Zero explanation after 6,000 years.

quiz.question: What makes the Carnac stone alignments mysterious?
options: They contain inscriptions in an undeciphered language
Nobody knows their purpose despite 6,000 years of existence
They were moved from a quarry over 500 miles away

hook.text: An Irish stone tomb was built so precisely that sunlight floods its inner chamber for exactly 17 minutes once a year.

buildup.text: Newgrange was built around 3200 BCE — 500 years before the Great Pyramid. It is a circular mound covering an acre.

discovery.text: A narrow slot above the entrance lets sunlight reach the back chamber only during the winter solstice sunrise.

twist.text: The passage tomb was sealed and forgotten for 4,000 years. When it was reopened in 1699, nobody knew who built it.

climax.text: The kerbstones outside are carved with spirals and lozenges whose meaning remains unknown — Europe's oldest monumental.

punchline.text: Five thousand years ago, farmers in Ireland built a solar clock more precise.

quiz.question: What happens at Newgrange during the winter solstice?
options: The entire mound is illuminated by reflected moonlight
Sunlight floods the inner chamber for exactly 17 minutes through a narrow slot
Shadows from the standing stones point directly at the entrance

topics.title: The Orkney Islands: Scotland's Hidden Civilization

hook.text: A storm in 1850 ripped turf off a Scottish hillside and revealed a 5,000-year-old village — complete with stone.

buildup.text: Skara Brae on Orkney had stone beds, dressers, and storage boxes built into the walls.

discovery.text: Each house had the same layout: a central hearth, two box beds, and a dresser facing the door — a standardized floor.

twist.text: Nearby, the Ness of Brodgar was discovered — a massive ceremonial complex suggesting Orkney was a major cultural center.

climax.text: Some archaeologists now believe the ideas behind Stonehenge originated in Orkney and traveled south.

punchline.text: A tiny Scottish island may have taught the rest of Britain how to build.

quiz.question: What controversial theory has emerged about Orkney's role in prehistory?
options: Orkney was settled by Egyptian colonists who brought pyramid knowledge
Ideas behind Stonehenge may have originated in Orkney and traveled south
Orkney was the capital of a prehistoric maritime empire

hook.text: Nearly 900 giant stone heads stand on a remote Pacific island. The tallest is 33 feet and weighs 82 tons.

buildup.text: The Rapa Nui people carved moai from volcanic tuff and moved them miles to platforms ringing the coastline.

discovery.text: Experiments proved that moai could 'walk' — rocked back and forth with ropes by as few as 18 people.

twist.text: The popular story blames the Rapa Nui for deforesting their island.

climax.text: European slave raids and disease in the 1800s nearly wiped out the Rapa Nui.

punchline.text: We blamed the islanders for their own collapse.

quiz.question: What does new evidence suggest about Easter Island's deforestation?
options: The Rapa Nui deliberately burned forests for farmland
Rats introduced by settlers destroyed the trees, not the people
A volcanic eruption killed all vegetation on the island

topics.title: Göbekli Tepe: The Temple Before Farming

hook.text: In Turkey, hunter-gatherers built a massive stone temple 11,600 years ago — before they learned to farm.

buildup.text: Göbekli Tepe has carved T-shaped pillars up to 18 feet tall, decorated with lions, vultures, and scorpions.

discovery.text: There are no houses, no water source, and no permanent residents. It was built purely for ritual gatherings.

twist.text: The site was deliberately buried around 8000 BCE. Someone filled it with rubble on purpose. Nobody knows why.

climax.text: Göbekli Tepe flipped archaeology's biggest assumption: people did not settle first and then build temples.

punchline.text: Religion may have invented civilization. Not the other way around.

quiz.question: How did Göbekli Tepe change archaeological thinking?
options: It proved farming was invented in Turkey, not the Fertile Crescent
It showed that monumental temples were built before permanent settlements
It revealed that writing existed thousands of years earlier than believed
